channel.title: Xiaoyuan — Systems Writing
channel.description: Writing about distributed data systems, ML platforms, and AI agents.

item.title: Agent Runtime 10: Who Should Execute a Subtask?
item.description: Choose an execution primitive for a subproblem from a Plan or Agent Loop by examining state ownership, durability, cancellation, and result consumption.

item.title: Agent Memory 5: Retrieval Cannot Rank by Similarity Alone
item.description: Start from currently valid facts and combine keyword, vector, hybrid search, and reranking instead of optimizing similarity alone.

item.title: Agent Runtime 4: Make the Event Log the Source of Truth
item.description: An ordered Session Event Log unifies execution facts while messages, Run state, and realtime events become rebuildable projections.

item.title: Agent Runtime 8: Receive Steering through a Durable Inbox
item.description: New input during execution and the race at Run completion show why an Agent Runtime needs a durable steering inbox with explicit consumption.

item.title: Context Engineering 4: How Model Routing Falls Back Safely
item.description: An explainable model-selection policy makes explicit which execution state remains reusable after fallback.

item.title: Agent Runtime 3: Isolate Product Policy with RunSpec
item.description: A RunSpec compiled before execution separates Profile policy from Runtime mechanism and keeps product branches out of the Agent Loop.

item.title: Agent Runtime 5: A Checkpoint Is Not an Object Snapshot
item.description: Design a versioned, recoverable, and explainable Agent Checkpoint without pretending that it guarantees fully deterministic replay.

item.title: Agent Security 1: Carry Identity through the Call Chain
item.description: A file update that crosses a queue shows how an agent can still prove who is acting for whom when execution resumes asynchronously.

item.title: Agent Runtime 1: Why a while Loop Is Not Enough
item.description: One Tool write with an unknown outcome shows why a simple Agent Loop can lose track of the task's actual state.

item.title: Agent Runtime 12: Define an Execution Contract for Middleware Hooks
item.description: A conflict among policy, request transformation, and tracing shows why Agent Runtime Hooks need explicit mutation, short-circuit, error, and replay semantics.

item.title: Agent Runtime 2: The State Layers of an Agent Execution
item.description: A PDF-report Task shows how completion ownership and retry boundaries separate Task, Run, Model Turn, Tool Execution, and Job, then maps those layers to OpenAI, Anthropic, and pi terminology.

item.title: Agent Tools 4: Tool Calls Need a Complete Lifecycle
item.description: A file write shows why a Tool needs a complete lifecycle across model selection, trusted execution, and result delivery.

item.title: Context Engineering 1: Context Assembly Is Not Message Concatenation
item.description: Conflicting history, memory, and files show why Context Assembly cannot be just message concatenation.

item.title: Agent Security 4: Treat External Content as Data, Not Instructions
item.description: Agents can read web pages, files, and email without letting their text expand the Task's authority.

item.title: Context Engineering 3: Manage Long Conversations with Incremental Compression
item.description: Use checkpoint summaries, incremental compression, and source backlinks to manage long conversations.

item.title: Agent Runtime 6: Choose Recovery at the Failure Boundary
item.description: A report-generation task amplified by retries at several layers shows how a Runtime should choose retry, fallback, repair, replan, or reconciliation from the failure owner, result certainty, and side-effect boundary.

item.title: Context Engineering 5: Isolate Provider Differences behind Adapters
item.description: A canonical contract and Provider Adapter keep prompt, Tool Schema, message, and streaming-event differences out of Runtime business logic.

item.title: Agent Runtime 7: Live Output Is Not an Execution Record
item.description: Separate recoverable execution events from low-latency notifications so that SSE or WebSocket is not mistaken for a source of truth.

item.title: Agent Runtime 9: Make Plans Safely Revisable
item.description: A research plan that keeps running after its premise fails shows how Plan revisions, execution facts, evidence, and delegation proposals should remain separate.

item.title: Agent Runtime 13: Own Concurrent Work with Structured Concurrency
item.description: A group of ownerless Tool `asyncio.Task` objects shows how TaskGroup makes concurrent work awaitable, cancellable, and able to propagate failures.

item.title: Context Engineering 2: How Context Should Degrade under Budget Pressure
item.description: Replace tail truncation with source quotas, priorities, and layered degradation when Context exceeds its budget.

item.title: Agent Runtime 11: How a Spawn Request Becomes a Controlled Child Run
item.description: How the Runtime validates a Spawn Request, creates a Child Run, and constrains its context, capabilities, budget, cancellation, and result collection.

item.title: Agent Memory 6: Tier Memory into Pinned, Hot, and Cold Views
item.description: Memory should not enter every prompt in full; classify its visibility before assembling it within the current budget.

item.title: Agent Memory 7: How Prompt Injection Enters Long-Term Memory
item.description: Trace how one external injection is miswritten as a user preference and persists across future Sessions.

item.title: Agent Memory 2: What Deserves Long-Term Retention?
item.description: A temporary location mistaken for a permanent residence motivates explicit write gates for information that should survive across Sessions.

item.title: Agent Memory 3: Isolate Write Authority by Writer
item.description: A background consolidation job that overrules an explicit preference shows why Memory mutation authority must follow writer identity, evidence, and action.

item.title: Agent Tools 3: Assemble a Tool Surface for Each Task
item.description: Select eager, deferred, and disabled capabilities from a Tool registry by task and permission, then evaluate the trade-offs in tokens, latency, and discovery recall.

item.title: Agent Memory 8: Memory Evaluation Needs More Than Recall
item.description: Evaluate whether Memory should be written, remains current, can be revoked, and stays within scope—not only whether it can be recalled.

item.title: Agent Tools 2: One Tool or Several?
item.description: Split Tools by user-distinguishable intent, permission, and side effects—not by backend endpoints.

item.title: Agent Tools 8: Why Tool Validation Drifts
item.description: Why the same Tool Schema may accept different arguments after provider adapters and executors, and how contract tests keep its semantics stable.

item.title: Agent Memory 4: Use Version Chains for Correction and Revocation
item.description: Version chains, a current view, and conditional writes make long-term Memory explainable, correctable, and safe under concurrent mutation.

item.title: Agent Memory 1: Why RAG Cannot Replace Memory
item.description: A repeatedly retrieved stale preference reveals the difference between historical text retrieval and governed long-term user state.

item.title: Agent Observability 1: Define the Grain before Modeling
item.description: A Tool retry shows why an Agent Task, Run, Model Turn, Tool Execution, and Attempt cannot share one row of analytical data.

item.title: State Machines, Leases, and Idempotency for Long-Running Tasks
item.description: Reliable long-running tasks depend on explicit state machines, expiring ownership, fencing tokens, and idempotent side effects—not on avoiding retries.

item.title: Agent Tools 1: Tool Schemas Are Model-Facing APIs
item.description: A tool schema is not a copy of a backend DTO. It is an interface that helps a model select a capability, generate arguments, and recover from errors.

item.title: Notes on Spark Adaptive Query Execution
item.description: Adaptive Query Execution lets Spark SQL revise its physical plan using runtime statistics, including coalescing shuffle partitions, handling skewed joins, and changing join strategies.

item.title: How to Use Spark Transformations Correctly
item.description: A Spark transformation describes lazy, distributed, recomputable work. Using transformations correctly requires understanding actions, closures, side effects, shuffles, partitions, and persistence.

item.title: Spark Data Skew — How to Identify, Diagnose, and Fix It
item.description: Data skew is not simply a slow job. It is an imbalance in how data is distributed across partitions. This article uses the Spark UI, key distributions, and execution plans to diagnose and address skew in joins and aggregations.

item.title: Notes on Spark Resource Requests and Data Representation on YARN
item.description: A practical example of Spark resource-request settings on YARN, followed by considerations for data representation in Spark.

item.title: Apache Spark Resource Management on YARN
item.description: An overview of Apache Spark resource management and the application model used when Spark runs on YARN.

item.title: Understanding Linux Process Memory Usage
item.description: A concise guide to VSS, RSS, PSS, and USS when inspecting the memory usage of a Linux process.

item.title: CMD or ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile?
item.description: CMD and ENTRYPOINT serve similar purposes in a Dockerfile, but their behavior—especially when combined—requires careful attention.

item.title: Why Use Tini as a Docker Container Entrypoint?
item.description: What is Tini, and why is it useful as the entrypoint of a container?

item.title: A New Beginning
item.description: Starting again with notes on technology and personal reflections.
